claim: $1,000 (in 1999 dollars) buys human-brain computational capacity (2019; restated as 2020 in a 2005 Q&A)

strict.criterion: A circa-$1,000 consumer budget, inflation-adjusted from 1999, buys approximately 20 petaflops of ordinary arithmetic capacity.
strict.rationale: Consumer hardware in 2019 was orders of magnitude below 20 petaflops in conventional FP32 throughput. Current checked consumer GPU specifications remain far short on that basis. Inflation adjustment and GPU-only accounting do not rescue the order-of-magnitude mismatch.

evidence.title: NVIDIA: RTX 30-series launch specifications and pricing
evidence.note: RTX 3080 launch price $699 and roughly 30 FP32 shader TFLOPS. Tensor, ray-tracing and shader operations are not interchangeable.

evidence.title: NVIDIA: RTX 5080 specifications
evidence.note: 10,752 CUDA cores, 2.62 GHz boost; theoretical FP32 about 56.3 TFLOPS using 2 operations/core/cycle. AI TOPS use different precision and cannot establish brain equivalence.

evidence.title: NVIDIA: Blackwell GeForce RTX 50-series launch
evidence.note: RTX 5080 launch MSRP $999, 1,801 AI TOPS. Launch prices are not represented as October 2026 retail quotes; a GPU also is not a whole PC.

broader.criterion: A circa-$1,000 consumer computer supplies roughly 10^16–2×10^16 calculations per second under either nominal or 1999-adjusted dollars.
broader.rationale: Even allowing inflation adjustment (roughly $1,500–$1,900 nominal) or the 2005 Q&A's 10^16 cps / 2020 phrasing, consumer GPUs in 2019–2020 (~30 FP32 TFLOPS) and 2025 (~56 FP32 TFLOPS; 1,801 sparse AI TOPS) remain orders of magnitude below 10^16–2×10^16 conventional operations per second.
changedConditions: Allows inflation adjustment and the lower 10^16 cps / 2020 Q&A wording; still fails by orders of magnitude
